01-hongshan.title: Hongshan: images before written legends
01-hongshan.summary: In north-eastern China, nephrite was carved into pendants, animals and coiled animal-like figures later called ‘pig-dragons’.
01-hongshan.detail: Archaeological finds reveal sophisticated working techniques and a connection between some objects and burials. The figures’ precise meaning remains debated: a modern name for a shape is not an ancient caption and does not establish a single shared mythology.
01-hongshan.place: Liaoning and Inner Mongolia, north-eastern China

02-liangzhu.title: Liangzhu: jade as a system of power
02-liangzhu.summary: In the Yangtze delta, bi discs, tubular cong and other forms were included in richly furnished burials.
02-liangzhu.detail: Differences in the quantity and quality of jades between burials help archaeologists identify social and ritual hierarchies. The purposes of individual forms are reconstructed from their find contexts; later texts cannot simply be projected onto the Neolithic.

03-shang-zhou.title: Shang and Zhou: ritual, rank and virtue
03-shang-zhou.summary: Jade objects accompanied ceremonies, elite dress, gift exchange and burial.
03-shang-zhou.detail: In later written traditions, the qualities of jade became a language of moral comparison: purity, steadfastness and nobility. This philosophical reading matters in its own right, but does not necessarily explain the original meaning of every earlier form.
03-shang-zhou.place: China’s Central Plains and neighbouring regions

04-mesoamerica.title: Mesoamerica: the green of life
04-mesoamerica.summary: The Olmec, and later the Maya, made jadeite masks, pendants, beads and emblems of royal power.
04-mesoamerica.detail: For the Maya, bright green material was associated with young maize, water, breath and renewal. These traditions developed independently of Chinese traditions; the shared European word jade does not imply a shared origin for their symbols.
04-mesoamerica.place: Southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras

05-qin-han.title: Qin and Han: empire and hopes of preservation
05-qin-han.summary: Elites included jade in elaborate funerary arrangements; surviving suits consist of plaques joined by wire.
05-qin-han.detail: Texts and archaeology record beliefs in jade’s purifying and preserving powers. The state of the buried bodies does not demonstrate that these beliefs were literally effective: the suits are evidence of ritual, status and technology.

06-medieval.title: From the Six Dynasties to the Yuan: new subjects
06-medieval.summary: Jade retained its prestige, while forms and subjects changed alongside court culture, religions and contacts across regions.
06-medieval.detail: Collections from this period include ornaments, vessels and objects for the scholar’s studio. Later makers also revisited ancient forms, so an archaic appearance alone does not guarantee an early date.

07-ming-qing.title: Ming and Qing: collecting and virtuosity
07-ming-qing.summary: Imperial collections brought together ancient jades, archaistic works and technically ambitious contemporary carving.
07-ming-qing.detail: Under the Qing, vivid jadeite from Myanmar gained considerable prestige. The Jadeite Cabbage shows how a carver turned natural green and white areas, cracks and inclusions into a convincing plant; some of its proposed wedding symbolism remains a matter of interpretation.

08-modern.title: The modern era: two materials, one name
08-modern.summary: Mineralogy distinguished nephrite from jadeite, while archaeology reconsidered museum dates and contexts.
08-modern.detail: Today, laboratories distinguish materials through composition, structure and instrumental analysis. At the same time, communities retain their own living concepts, such as Māori pounamu, which cannot be reduced to a single gemmological classification.

01-heshi-bi.title: Mr He’s jade
01-heshi-bi.legend: In China Culture’s retelling, Bian He twice offers rulers an unworked stone and is twice punished as a deceiver. Under a third ruler, the find is worked and its precious core revealed. The stone’s name becomes a recognition of the man’s honesty.
01-heshi-bi.context: The story is known through ancient texts and later retellings; over time, the legendary disc became associated with diplomatic narratives and the imperial seal.
01-heshi-bi.confirmed: The textual tradition exists, and bi discs are known archaeologically. But no particular object has been identified as Heshibi: its fate and transformation into a seal belong to the legendary account.

02-han-immortality.title: Jade against decay
02-han-immortality.legend: Jade was believed to purify and preserve the body, so high-ranking people could be buried in suits made of hundreds or thousands of plaques.
02-han-immortality.context: Burial was understood as a place where status and existence continued. The material, labour and complexity of the suit also expressed the family’s power.
02-han-immortality.confirmed: Archaeologists have found suits and plaques; museum research documents beliefs about preservation. The biological preservation of bodies does not substantiate the claimed power of the stone.

03-poutini.title: Poutini — guardian of pounamu
03-poutini.legend: In one iwi pūrākau, the supernatural Poutini guards Ngāhue and the spiritual essence of pounamu, while his journey along the West Coast explains places associated with the stone.
03-poutini.context: Different iwi have different accounts of the origins of pounamu. The narrative connects landscape, genealogy, rights and community memory.
03-poutini.confirmed: Pounamu is indeed sourced mainly from the South Island and has particular significance for Ngāi Tahu. The mythological layer is presented as a living tradition, not a geological explanation.

04-maya-breath.title: The stone of living breath
04-maya-breath.legend: Lustrous, cool jadeite was associated with water, mist, young maize and the breath of life; a bead could be placed in the mouth of an elite deceased person as a sign of eternal life.
04-maya-breath.context: Its green colour, rare source in the Motagua valley and labour-intensive working made jadeite a material of power, inheritance and the sacred centre.
04-maya-breath.confirmed: Archaeological finds, imagery and inscriptions attest to elite and funerary use. The phrase ‘living stone’ describes a cultural concept, not a physical property of the mineral.

nephrite.name: Nephrite
nephrite.family: An amphibole rock of the tremolite–actinolite series
nephrite.toughness: Exceptionally high; nephrite usually resists chipping better than jadeite
nephrite.note: Nephrite can be white, grey, yellow, brown or green. Iron influences its green shades, but colour alone cannot establish authenticity: reliable identification requires gemmological and spectroscopic methods.

jadeite.name: Jadeite
jadeite.family: A pyroxene rock composed mainly of jadeite
jadeite.structure: A dense mosaic of interlocking mineral grains
jadeite.toughness: Very high, although fibrous nephrite usually resists impact better
jadeite.note: Jadeite is not a variety of nephrite, but a different mineralogical material. Both have historically been called jade; the highly prized translucent green examples represent only a small part of jadeite’s rich palette.

01-healing-energy.title: The stone’s ‘healing energy’
01-healing-energy.tradition: Nephrite has been credited with protection, longevity, purification and support for the life force. These beliefs matter as part of cultural and religious history.
01-healing-energy.assessment: There is no reliable clinical evidence that nephrite’s chemical composition itself treats disease or transfers a special energy to people. Evidence on rollers and gua sha tests the mechanical effects of the procedures, not a healing property of the stone.
01-healing-energy.safety: Do not replace diagnosis, medication or prescribed treatment with a stone. Seek advice from a medical professional for new, severe or persistent symptoms.

02-roller-circulation.title: Facial rollers and skin microcirculation
02-roller-circulation.tradition: Cool, smooth tools are used for facial massage, to ease the feeling of puffiness and for relaxation.
02-roller-circulation.assessment: A small Japanese study recorded a short-term increase in skin blood flow after five minutes of roller massage. It involved 12–14 people, and the roller material was not specific to nephrite: the result cannot support claims about a special power of the mineral.
02-roller-circulation.safety: Use a clean tool without strong pressure; do not use it on damaged, inflamed or infected skin. Stop if it causes pain or irritation.

03-gua-sha-pain.title: Gua sha and muscle pain
03-gua-sha-pain.tradition: Gua sha is a technique that scrapes the skin with a smooth tool. Stone plates are often used today, although tool materials have varied historically.
03-gua-sha-pain.assessment: A systematic review by Korean researchers found too few high-quality trials to establish the effectiveness of gua sha for pain. Short-term relief is possible, but confidence in the effect and its causes remains low.
03-gua-sha-pain.safety: Gua sha can cause petechiae, bruising and soreness. Do not use it on damaged skin or when there is a risk of bleeding; if you take anticoagulants, consult a doctor first.

04-cosmetic-effect.title: Short-term cosmetic effects
04-cosmetic-effect.tradition: Facial massage with a roller or gua sha tool is promoted as a way to improve contour, firmness and skin appearance.
04-cosmetic-effect.assessment: A small randomised study in 2025 involving 34 women reported changes in selected measures after eight weeks of home massage. It compared two active techniques without a group receiving no treatment, so it does not demonstrate lasting rejuvenation or isolate the effect of nephrite as a material.
04-cosmetic-effect.safety: Maintain good hygiene, avoid excessive pressure and do not expect massage to replace dermatological treatment. If you develop persistent swelling, a rash or pain, stop the massage and consult a doctor.
